Writing questions

Source: vignettes/writing-questions.Rmd
writing-questions.Rmd
library(layaR)

Laya answers questions it has never seen before: you describe the decision in plain language and the model reads your wording. How you word a question therefore matters. This vignette covers the three question types, what makes a question work well, and the token budget a question’s options share.

The three question types

Choice: one label from a set

Each option is a label, optionally with a description after =. The label comes back as the answer, so make it meaningful; the description tells the model what the label covers.

dept <- laya_choice(
  "Which department should handle this request?",
  billing   = "invoices, payments, refunds",
  technical = "bugs, outages, system errors",
  sales     = "pricing, new contracts",
  other     = "everything else"
)
dept
#> <laya_question> choice Which department should handle this request?  [4 options: billing, technical, sales, other]

Labels alone work too, when they are self-explanatory:

laya_choice("What is the message about?", "shipping", "returns", "product question")
#> <laya_question> choice What is the message about?  [3 options: shipping, returns, product question]

If the options live in a vector already, pass them with .options:

teams <- c(billing = "invoices, refunds", technical = "bugs, outages")
laya_choice("Which team?", .options = teams)
#> <laya_question> choice Which team?  [2 options: billing, technical]

Score: a position on an ordinal scale

Give the levels from lowest to highest. The answer is the expected level: a number between 0 and the number of levels minus one, so 1.6 on a three-level scale sits between the middle and the top level.

urgency <- laya_score("How urgent is this request?",
                      c("not urgent", "soon", "critical deadline or blocking issue"))

Noul: yes or no

A statement that is either true or false about the state. The answer is the calibrated probability that it holds. if_false and if_true can say what each side means when that isn’t obvious:

phishing <- laya_noul("Is this email a phishing attempt?",
                      if_false = "a legitimate email",
                      if_true = "phishing or fraud")

Question sets

laya_questions() combines questions; the argument names become the answer ids. All the questions in a set are answered in one forward pass.

qs <- laya_questions(department = dept, urgency = urgency,
                     churn_risk = laya_noul("Does the customer say they will cancel or leave?"))

Sets combine with c(), and [ selects questions by id:

more <- c(qs, laya_questions(phishing = phishing))
names(more)
#> [1] "department" "urgency"    "churn_risk" "phishing"
names(more[c("urgency", "phishing")])
#> [1] "urgency"  "phishing"

laya_validate_questions() checks a set with the engine’s own rules, without loading a model:

shared <- '{"team": {"type": "choice", "instructions": "Which team?",
                     "criteria": ["billing", "support", "billing"]}}'
try(laya_validate_questions(shared))
#> Error in laya_validate_questions(shared) : 
#>   question 'team': choice label 2 ('billing') repeats an earlier label

Writing questions that work

Make each option self-contained. The model sees the options, not your database. “billing: invoices, payments, refunds” works; “team_7” does not. Put the fact that distinguishes an option near the start of its label or description.

Option order matters. The model scores one marker per option, in order, and position alone shifts the scores: upstream measured a clear lean toward the first options when every option reads the same. A clear-cut text gets the same answer in any order, but an ambiguous one may not. Here the same three options are asked in two orders:

options_a <- c(billing = "invoices, payments, refunds", technical = "bugs, outages, login",
               sales = "pricing, new contracts")
options_b <- options_a[c("sales", "technical", "billing")]
ask <- function(text) {
  qs <- laya_questions(
    order_a = laya_choice("Which department should handle this request?", .options = options_a),
    order_b = laya_choice("Which department should handle this request?", .options = options_b)
  )
  laya_predict(text, qs) |> as.data.frame() |> subset(select = c(id, answer, value))
}
ask("We want to upgrade to 50 seats but the payment form keeps failing.")
#>        id  answer  value
#> 1 order_a billing 0.9994
#> 2 order_b billing 0.9998
ask("The app shows the wrong price at checkout.")
#>        id  answer  value
#> 1 order_a billing 0.9999
#> 2 order_b   sales 0.9998

The second message could reasonably go to billing or to sales, and the answer follows whichever of the two is listed first. When a wrong answer is costly, ask in a couple of orders on your own examples, and treat answers that change with the order as uncertain. Put a catch-all such as “other” last. The probabilities always come back keyed by your labels, whatever the order.

Ask about the state, not the world. “Does the customer say they will cancel?” is answerable from the text; “Will the customer cancel?” asks the model to guess. Negated wording (“Is this not spam?”) is a known weak spot; prefer the positive statement and read 1 - p if you need the opposite.

Reword a question that misses. Small changes in wording can matter a lot. Here three wordings of the same yes/no question are asked about texts where the answer is known:

texts <- c(
  "Duplicate charge. We were billed twice for March. Refund it or we cancel.",
  "Your service has been unreliable for months. Please close my account.",
  "Please refund the duplicate today or we will cancel our plan.",
  "Since the last update the app closes as soon as I log in.",
  "We're a team of 50 and want a quote for the annual plan."
)
truth <- c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE)
wordings <- laya_questions(
  threaten = laya_noul("Does the user threaten to cancel or leave?"),
  say      = laya_noul("Does the customer say they will cancel or leave?"),
  mention  = laya_noul("Does the customer mention cancelling their plan, subscription or account?")
)
p <- laya_predict_batch(texts, wordings) |>
  sapply(function(r) vapply(r$answers, function(a) a$noul, numeric(1)))
data.frame(cancels = truth, round(t(p), 2))
#>   cancels threaten  say mention
#> 1    TRUE     0.02 0.80    0.97
#> 2    TRUE     0.18 0.99    0.96
#> 3    TRUE     0.03 0.68    0.98
#> 4   FALSE     0.01 0.43    0.64
#> 5   FALSE     0.01 0.03    0.00

“Threaten” misses every cancellation. “Say they will” gets all five right, though the crash report sits closer to 0.5 than you might like. “Mention” scores the cancellations highest but also flags the crash report. No wording is perfect, and the only way to know is to measure: keep a handful of labelled examples like these for each question you rely on, and check every new wording against them.

Keep a choice to about 20 options. All the options of a question share a fixed token budget (below). With many more, each option gets only a few tokens and they stop being distinguishable. Split a large label set into a coarse question and a fine one instead.

Check calibration on your data before gating. Confidence is calibrated on the training distribution. Before relying on min_confidence, look at a few dozen labelled examples from your own workflow and check that the answers given with high confidence are mostly right.

The token budget

A checkpoint reads at most max_len tokens: your options (the “head”) and the state share them. The options may use up to head_max_len tokens; the state gets what’s left. laya_engine_info() shows the budgets:

info <- laya_engine_info(laya_default_engine())
info[c("checkpoint", "max_len", "head_max_len")]
#> $checkpoint
#> [1] "multilingual"
#> 
#> $max_len
#> [1] 1024
#> 
#> $head_max_len
#> [1] 256

A state too long for the room left is truncated, and the result says so:

long_text <- strrep("The invoice was wrong again. ", 400)
res <- laya_predict(long_text, qs)
str(res$usage[c("input_tokens", "truncated")])
#> List of 2
#>  $ input_tokens: int 3072
#>  $ truncated   : logi TRUE

For long documents, use laya_predict_long(), which scans the text in overlapping windows (see vignette("data-frames", package = "layaR")).

If the options don’t fit at all, the call fails with a laya_error_no_markers error you can catch:

tryCatch(
  laya_predict("Hello", qs, max_len = 32),
  laya_error_no_markers = function(e) cat("Options don't fit:", conditionMessage(e), "\n")
)
#> Options don't fit: question 'department': only 3 of its 4 option markers fit in max_len=32 with
#> head_max_len=256 spent on the question; lower head_max_len, raise max_len, or use fewer
#> options

max_len and head_max_len can be raised per call (up to 8192), which helps when a question has many long options. The checkpoints were trained at their shipped budgets, so measure accuracy on your own examples if you change them.

Sharing questions with Python

Question sets are stored in the Python SDK’s format, so they move between the two languages unchanged:

cat(laya_questions_to_json(qs["churn_risk"]))
#> {
#>   "churn_risk": {
#>     "type": "noul",
#>     "instructions": "Does the customer say they will cancel or leave?"
#>   }
#> }
path <- tempfile(fileext = ".json")
laya_questions_to_json(qs, path)
identical(as_laya_questions(path), qs)
#> [1] TRUE

as_laya_questions() also reads a JSON string or a list in the same format.
